'''''Ulex gallii''''', the '''western gorse''' or '''dwarf furze'''<ref>A R Clapham, T G Tutin, E F Warburg, ''Flora of the British Isles'', Cambridge, 1962, p. 332</ref> is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] in the pea family ([[Fabaceae]]), native to the Atlantic coasts of western [[Europe]]: southern [[Scotland]], [[England]], [[Wales]], [[Ireland]], the [[Isle of Man]], western [[France]] and the northern coast of [[Green Spain|Spain]].
[[Image:Ulex gallii bush.jpg|thumb|200px|left|''Ulex gallii'' growing on the flanks of [[Snowdon]]]]
It favours [[acid]]ic heathy soils and is frequently found in exposed maritime and montane environments.  It is more common in the west of its distribution; in eastern England it is replaced in similar habitats by the closely related Dwarf Furze (''[[Ulex minor]]''), with very little overlap in the distribution of the two species.


==Description==
{{citations needed|date=October 2025}}
''Ulex gallii'' is usually {{Convert|10|to|50|cm|in|sigfig=1}} tall although it may grow up to {{Convert|2|m|ft|sigfig=1}}. The stems are modified into [[spine (botany)|spine]]s, mostly about {{Convert|1|cm|in|sigfig=1}} long, but with some regularly spaced recurved spines of about {{Convert|3|cm|in|sigfig=1}}.  Like other members of the genus ''[[Ulex]]'' it has trifoliate leaves as a seedling, but later the leaves are reduced to small scales or spines. The stems are green, and almost wholly replace the leaves as the plant's functioning [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic]] organs.

The [[flower]]s are yellow, {{Convert|1|to|2|cm|in|sigfig=1}} long, with the typical [[pea]]-flower structure; they are produced principally in the late summer and autumn, rarely before July. The [[fruit]] is a [[legume]] (pod), partly enclosed by the pale brown remnants of the flower.

Like many species of [[Ulex|gorse]], it can grow as a [[wildfire|fire]]-climax plant, which readily catches fire but re-grows from the [[root]]s after the fire; the seeds are also adapted to germinate after slight scorching by fire.
